title: TSPi Team Workbook  -  TMA3084 Software Engineering Laboratory
subtitle: Faculty of Computer Science & Information Technology, UNIMAS   |   Semester 1, Session 2026/2027   |   Workbook v3.0 (2026-10-29)
author: Ts. Nurfauza Jali, FCSIT UNIMAS

about.label: What this is
about.text: A Team Software Process (TSP) team workbook rebuilt for TMA3084. It keeps the TSP measurement discipline - time, defects, size, earned value - and adds the forms this course actually assesses: AI-assisted coding, automated testing, GitHub workflow, client engagement and peer evaluation.

about.label: Lineage
about.text: The process model follows the Team Software Process introduced by Watts S. Humphrey. The original TSPi support workbook (2002, Addison-Wesley) is the ancestor of this file; every sheet here has been rewritten for this course. Forms, phases, defect types and all guidance text are original to TMA3084.

about.label: What changed from the 2002 workbook
about.text: NEW forms: LOGAI (AI-assisted development), LOGTEST (test cases), LOGCLIENT (client meetings), LOGGIT (GitHub activity), CCR (change requests), PEER, TEAMEVAL, ASSESS, DASHBOARD, FORM-SI.  MODERNISED: phase set now covers AI generation, pull-request review, static analysis, widget test and CI/CD; defect types extended with UI/Layout, State Management, Performance, Security and AI-Generated; size measures cover screens, widgets and API endpoints alongside LOC.  REMOVED: the single-week WEEK form is now a 13-week tracking table, and the PSP-style prediction intervals are dropped as the team has no historical data base.

about.label: Colour convention
about.text: AMBER cells are yours to fill in.  GREY cells are calculated - typing over one destroys the rollup.  Every drop-down is fed by the LISTS sheet.

about.label: How to run it
about.text: 1. Fill SETUP once, then FORM-SI with every member.  2. Agree roles in ROLES and goals in GOALS.  3. Plan each cycle in TASK and SCHEDULE.  4. Record daily in LOGT, LOGD, LOGTEST and LOGAI.  5. Hold the weekly meeting against WEEK and IRTL.  6. SUMP, SUMQ, SUMS and DASHBOARD fill themselves.

about.label: One workbook per team
about.text: The team keeps one shared copy in the repository (docs/tspi/). Each member records their own rows in the logs and tags them with their name, so individual contribution is traceable without separate files.

about.label: Honesty clause
about.text: These numbers are the evidence behind Peer/Individual and Team Evaluation. Logging work you did not do, or back-filling a term's worth of hours the night before a milestone, is academic dishonesty and the pattern is visible in DASHBOARD.

intro.label: The short version
intro.text: This is a Team Software Process (TSP) workbook. TSP is a way of running a software project where the team plans its own work, measures what actually happens, and uses those measurements to plan better next time. The workbook is where the measuring happens.

intro.label: Why bother
intro.text: Three questions decide most student projects: are we going to finish on time, is the thing we are building any good, and is everyone actually contributing. Opinions on all three are usually wrong. This workbook answers them with data the team collected itself.

intro.label: The four things you record
intro.text: TIME - how long work actually took, not how long it felt.   SIZE - how much you built.   DEFECTS - every mistake found, and the phase where it was made.   STATUS - which tasks are finished. Everything else on the summary sheets is arithmetic on those four.

intro.label: What it is not
intro.text: It is not a surveillance tool and it is not graded on neatness. Nobody is marked down for a high defect count - a team recording 40 defects is doing better engineering than an identical team recording 3, because the second team is not looking. What does get noticed is a log that is empty, or one filled in all at once the night before a milestone.

stages.title: 3.  Stage one  -  the launch  (do this in Week 1, and again at the start of every cycle)

steps.what: Course details, team name, project title, client, repository URL and team size. Then check the milestone dates against the course outline and set the thresholds. Every other sheet reads its header from here, so this is the one place you type the team name.

One row per member in FORM-SI: matric number, full name, UNIMAS email, GitHub handle. The name you type here is the name that appears in every drop-down, so agree on a spelling and do not change it later.

The lower half of FORM-SI. Six short answers: vision, communication norms, definition of done, conflict resolution, quality standards, expected hours. Write these before you disagree about them, not after.

There are six roles and five of you, so one member holds two this cycle and nobody holds more than two. The double rotates, and nobody keeps the same role for more than two milestones running. The Role Load Check at the bottom of the sheet adds this up for you. A role is real work, not a title.
A goal needs a number and an owner or it is a wish. Seven starter goals are listed at the bottom of the sheet; replace them with your own.

What each cycle actually delivers, what you build versus reuse, the main technical risk and who owns it. Then record the stack decisions and why - the Design rubric asks you to justify alternatives considered.
List the screens, modules and documents in SUMS with a planned size. Estimates will be wrong early on. Record them anyway - a wrong estimate you measured against is worth more than no estimate.
Tasks of roughly 2 to 10 hours, each with one owner, a phase, planned hours and a planned week. A task bigger than 10 hours is hiding something.
Put the hours each week in SCHEDULE. Check the Difference cell at the top: schedule hours must match task hours. If they do not, one of the two plans is fiction.

stages.title: 4.  Stage two  -  daily discipline  (the habit that makes everything else work)

steps.what: Start a LOGT row when you sit down, fill in the stop time when you get up. Subtract interruptions honestly. Reconstructing a week of hours from memory produces numbers that are worse than useless, because they look real.
Put the Task ID from TASK in the Task ID column. That is what makes hours roll up against the plan. Unplanned work with no ID is fine - add the task to TASK afterwards so the plan stays honest.

Anything wrong that you had to fix, including the ones you found yourself within a minute. The hard column is Injected in: the phase where the mistake was MADE, not where you noticed it. Getting that right is the whole point.
One row per test case with its type and status. Automated tests get a row too - LOGTEST is the evidence behind the Testing and Release rubric, not a duplicate of your test files.

Any time Copilot, Claude or another generator wrote code that reached the repository: what you asked for, how many lines it gave you, how many survived review, who reviewed it, and whether tests were written. The reviewer must not be you - the sheet turns that row red.

Date, mode, who attended, what was decided, what actions came out and who owns them. Keep the minutes or a photo as evidence. The milestones require 2, 4 and 6 cumulative meetings - this is how you prove it.

stages.title: 5.  Stage three  -  the weekly meeting  (about 30 minutes, same time every week)

steps.what: Commits, pull requests, reviews and issues closed per member, read from the repository Insights tab. These are facts - do not estimate them.
Mark finished tasks Complete. Earned value is only credited for completed tasks; a task that is 90% done earns nothing. That is deliberate - it is what stops a plan from slipping quietly.

WEEK fills itself from SCHEDULE. Look at EV variance: negative means the team has delivered less than it planned by this week, however many hours it has burned. Hours are effort; earned value is progress.
A risk might happen, an issue already has. Both need a likelihood, an impact, an owner and a follow-up date. Priority is calculated; anything scoring 6 or more goes red and gets discussed.
Once the client has agreed a baseline, changes go through CCR with an estimate and a decision - not through a quiet commit. This is also how scope creep becomes visible instead of mysterious.
Milestone readiness, effort, quality and contribution on one screen. Anything red is the agenda for the next ten minutes.

The contribution panel compares each member's hours, commits, reviews and AI entries against an even share. A flag is a prompt for a conversation, not an accusation - someone may be carrying work the logs do not capture, and if so, that is worth knowing too.
One line in WEEK saying what the team will have finished by the next meeting. Then check it at that meeting. This single habit does more for delivery than any tool.

stages.title: 6.  Stage four  -  closing a milestone  (the postmortem)

steps.what: Go back to SUMS and fill the actual columns, plus actual SRS and SDD pages. Without actual size there is no defect density and no productivity figure.
SUMP now shows where the time went, where defects were injected and where they were removed. Compare the Actual % column against your plan. The gap between them is the lesson.
SUMQ is where the uncomfortable truths live: review rates that were too fast, A/FR below 2.0, process yield under 70%. Each one predicts a specific kind of pain in the next cycle.
One manual cell on SUMQ, read from the coverage job in GitHub Actions. Do not estimate it.

Each member rates every member including themselves, 1 to 5, across the 10 rubric categories. Self-ratings are reported separately so they cannot inflate anyone's score. Rate what people did, not whether you like them.

Ten statements about how the team works, rated 1 to 5. Then look at the spread, not just the mean - where members disagree sharply is the thing worth discussing. Agree actions at the bottom of the sheet.
ASSESS maps every rubric to the forms that produce its evidence. Peer and Team Evaluation fill themselves; the rest are entered by the instructor.

Open CHARTS and read them as a team. The four that matter most are Cumulative Earned Value (did we deliver what we planned), Defects Removed by Phase (are we catching them early), Review Rates (did we read fast enough to miss things) and Process Yield (what reached test). A number on a sheet is arguable; a line going the wrong way for six weeks is not.

Not twenty. Pick three things the team will do differently next cycle, write them into GOALS with an owner, and check them at the next postmortem. A postmortem that changes nothing was just a meeting.

examples.situation: You spend the morning writing the SRS, with a 15-minute phone call in the middle
examples.record: LOGT: date 20-Oct-26, member your name, milestone M1, phase REQ, task ID T01, start 09:00, stop 12:00, interrupt 15. Delta calculates as 165 minutes. Week fills in by itself.

examples.situation: During the code review of a login screen, you find a null check that was never written
examples.record: LOGD: type 60 - Checking, component auth_module, injected in CODE (the mistake was made while coding), removed in CR (you found it in review), fix time 8 minutes, severity Major, from AI code No.

examples.situation: Copilot generates a form validator; you keep about three quarters of it after review
examples.record: LOGAI: tool GitHub Copilot, lines generated 60, lines kept 45, reviewer a teammate's name - not yours - verdict Approved with changes, tests written Yes, commit reference PR#7, approved Yes.

examples.situation: A test that passed last week now fails after a refactor
examples.record: LOGTEST: update that test's row to Fail with today's date. Then raise the defect in LOGD with injected phase CODE and removed phase UT, and link the two with the defect reference.

examples.situation: The client asks for an extra screen three weeks before release
examples.record: CCR: change type Requirement, what changes and why, estimated hours, affected milestone, reviewer and decision. If approved, add the tasks to TASK so the plan reflects reality.

troubleshooting.fix: FORM-SI has no names in it yet. Every member drop-down in the workbook reads column C of FORM-SI rows 9 to 14. Fill those first.

troubleshooting.symptom: A summary number has not changed after I logged work
troubleshooting.fix: Press F9, or close and reopen the file. If it still looks wrong, check the phase or task ID you typed in the log - a typo means the row matches nothing and is silently excluded.

troubleshooting.symptom: Hours are logged but TASK shows zero actual hours
troubleshooting.fix: The Task ID column in LOGT is blank or does not match an ID in TASK. The match is exact, so T1 and T01 are different tasks.

troubleshooting.symptom: Defect density and review rates are blank
troubleshooting.fix: SUMS has no actual size recorded, so there is nothing to divide by. Fill the actual columns in SUMS at the end of each milestone.

troubleshooting.symptom: Someone's peer score looks far too low
troubleshooting.fix: Check that every member filled in their own rating block. An empty block is ignored rather than counted as zero, but a block filled in for only some members will skew the average.

troubleshooting.symptom: A grey cell shows a wrong number and I want to correct it
troubleshooting.fix: Do not type over it. Find the log row that is wrong and fix that. Overwriting a calculated cell breaks the formula permanently and every number downstream of it.

troubleshooting.symptom: We forgot to log for two weeks
troubleshooting.fix: Reconstruct what you honestly can, mark those rows in the comments column, and say so at the weekly meeting. Inventing plausible numbers is worse than admitting a gap - the gap is recoverable, fabricated data quietly corrupts every conclusion the team draws for the rest of the project.

manual.closing: The workbook cannot make the team work well. What it can do is make it obvious, early and to everyone, when the team is not - while there is still time to do something about it. A team that logs honestly and looks at the numbers every week will finish; a team that fills this in the weekend before submission will have a very tidy record of a project that went wrong.

roles.owns: Runs the launch and the weekly meeting, keeps the team to its plan, owns the relationship with the instructor and demonstrator, reports status.
Owns the client relationship and the backlog. Books and chairs client meetings, turns client needs into prioritised user stories, obtains sign-off.
Owns the Flutter codebase and the architecture. Allocates implementation work, enforces the branching model and the pull-request review rule.
Owns TASK and SCHEDULE. Produces the plan, tracks earned value weekly, raises the alarm when the team drifts off plan.
Owns SUMQ, LOGD and LOGTEST - the review, inspection and test discipline. Tracks defect density, yield and coverage, chairs inspections, owns the AI-code review rule, and reports release readiness.
Owns the repository, CI/CD, environments, builds and configuration control. Maintains LOGGIT and the CCR log.

roleRule: There are six roles and five of you, so in every cycle exactly one member holds two roles and nobody holds more than two. The double role rotates - the same member does not carry it twice in a row - and every member holds a role in every cycle. No member may hold the same role for more than two consecutive milestones. Agree the rotation at the launch meeting and record it above; a change mid-cycle goes through the CCR log with the reason stated. If your team has four members, two of you will double up; the check above works that out from the team size.

phaseNotes: Scope:  S = the phase applies to the system as a whole.  P = it applies to one component.  N = neither.
Log time:  Y means sessions in this phase belong in LOGT.
Log injected / removed:  Y means LOGD may name this phase in the Injected in or Removed in column.
Counts as development:  Y means the phase feeds the development defect totals on SUMP and the yields on SUMQ.
Size basis:  what the phase's rate is measured against when SUMQ computes review rates.

defectTypes.name: Documentation
defectTypes.covers: Comments, README, API docs, user manual
defectTypes.example: A widget's doc comment describes the old behaviour after a refactor.

defectTypes.name: Syntax
defectTypes.example: Missing semicolon, misspelled identifier, wrong bracket.

defectTypes.name: Build / Package
defectTypes.covers: pubspec, dependency conflict, Gradle, signing, build config
defectTypes.example: pubspec version conflict; Gradle or signing config breaks the release build.

defectTypes.name: Assignment
defectTypes.covers: Declaration, duplicate names, scope, null-safety misuse
defectTypes.example: A nullable field used without a null check; two widgets sharing a class name.

defectTypes.name: Interface
defectTypes.covers: Procedure calls, REST/API contract, parameters, serialization
defectTypes.example: A repository returns a List where the caller awaits a Stream; JSON key mismatch.

defectTypes.name: Checking
defectTypes.covers: Error messages, input validation, inadequate checks
defectTypes.example: No validation on a quantity field; an empty list shows a spinner forever.

defectTypes.name: Data
defectTypes.covers: Structure, content, persistence, local DB / Firestore schema
defectTypes.example: Dates stored local but compared as UTC; a schema missing a sync-status column.

defectTypes.name: Function
defectTypes.covers: Logic, pointers, loops, recursion, computation, business rules
defectTypes.example: A total recalculated on add but not on edit; discount applied before tax.

defectTypes.name: System
defectTypes.example: Works on Android, fails on iOS; a timing problem only under slow network.

defectTypes.name: Environment
defectTypes.covers: Design, compile, test or other support system problems
defectTypes.example: The emulator, the CI runner or the toolchain itself is the problem.

defectTypes.name: UI / Layout
defectTypes.covers: Overflow, responsiveness, theming, accessibility, Material 3 misuse
defectTypes.example: RenderFlex overflow on a small screen; text unreadable at the counter's font setting.

defectTypes.name: State Management
defectTypes.covers: Provider/Riverpod/GetX misuse, rebuild storms, stale or lost state
defectTypes.example: setState after dispose; a filter that does not clear when a screen is reopened.

defectTypes.name: Performance
defectTypes.covers: Jank, frame drops, oversized images, unbounded list builds
defectTypes.example: A long list janks; an oversized image decoded on every rebuild.

defectTypes.name: Security
defectTypes.covers: Hard-coded API key, missing auth check, unsafe storage, leaked PII
defectTypes.example: An API key committed in source; a screen reachable without an auth check.

defectTypes.name: AI-Generated
defectTypes.covers: Defect traced to AI-generated code that passed review unverified
defectTypes.example: Generated code that passed review but was wrong - a validator accepting negatives.

defectTypeNote: Pick the type that describes the mistake, not the symptom. A crash caused by a missing null check is Assignment, not System. If a defect genuinely spans two types, choose the earlier one in the list - that is where the fix belongs. Type 150 is for a defect that reached the repository inside generated code: use it alongside the From AI code column in LOGD, because together they show whether the review rule is working.

notes.label: The first plan is a guess
notes.text: Your first cycle has no history, so the estimates below are a starting point, not a standard. Record what actually happens and the second plan will be built on your own numbers instead of someone else's.

notes.label: Effort per member
notes.text: Budget about 10 hours per member per week across a 13-week semester. For a five-person team that is roughly 600 team-hours for the whole project. If your plan totals far more than that, you are planning work the team cannot do.

notes.label: Task size
notes.text: Break work into tasks of 2 to 10 hours. Anything larger hides its own progress - you cannot tell a 20-hour task that is half done from one that has barely started.

notes.label: Rough shape of a cycle
notes.text: Requirements and design together should be about a third of the effort, implementation about a third, and test, documentation and management the rest. A plan that spends 70% on coding is a plan that will spend its last three weeks in test.

shares.phases: TD + BUILD + UT + WT + IT + ST

rates.why: Includes the thinking, not just the typing.

rates.rate: no faster than 10 pages per hour
rates.why: Faster than this and you stop finding defects.

rates.rate: no faster than 10 pages per hour

rates.why: New and changed lines, including the thinking.
Faster to produce, but the review is the real cost.

rates.rate: no faster than 200 LOC per hour
rates.why: The single most reliable number in TSP.
A case is a scenario, not a line of code.

planGuide.aiWarning: Generated code arrives faster than written code, and teams plan as though that speed carries through to delivery. It does not. The generator moves the work from writing to reviewing, and a team that plans for the first saving without planning for the second cost finds its defects in system test instead of in review. Plan AIGEN at a high rate and plan CR high to match it.

qualGuide.idea: A defect costs more the later you find it. One caught in a design review costs minutes; the same defect caught in system test costs hours; caught by the client it costs their trust. Every measure on SUMQ exists to answer one question: are you finding your defects early, or is the machine finding them for you late?

measures.below: You read too fast to find anything. The rate, not the hours, is what predicts how many defects a review catches - halve the rate before you add more reviewers.
Same problem on documents. An SRS inspection at 30 pages an hour finds typos, not missing requirements.
You are spending more time fixing in test than reviewing before it. This is the earliest reliable warning that system test will hurt.
Designs are going to code unreviewed. Defects injected in design are the expensive ones - they survive until integration.
Code is being merged on a glance. With AI-generated code in the repository this matters more, not less.
The team is typing before it is thinking. Expect rework.
Most of your defects are reaching test. Each one there costs several times what it would have cost in review.
Integration will be slow and unpredictable, because you are still finding unit-level defects there.
The client is about to become your tester. This is the number that decides whether handover goes well.
The absolute number matters less than the direction. A team whose test density rises cycle over cycle is reviewing less, not writing better.
Anything critical here was missed by every check you have. Work backwards and find which one.
Untested logic is not working logic, it is logic nobody has contradicted yet.
A suite that is often red stops being read. Fix or delete failing tests - never ignore them.
Every one of these is generated code merged on trust. This is the single rule most worth enforcing.

qualGuide.fixOrder: If several measures are red, fix them in this order: review rate first, because it is the cheapest change and it moves everything downstream; then design review time, because design defects are the costly ones; then coverage. Do not start by adding testers - testing finds defects later and more expensively than reviewing does, and a team that responds to poor quality by testing harder is paying the highest price available for the same information.

member.title: My TSPi Workbook  -  TMA3084 Software Engineering Laboratory

about.label: What this is
about.text: Your own copy of the TSPi workbook. You record your work here - your time, your defects, your tests, your AI-assisted changes - and nobody else types in this file.

about.label: How it fits together
about.text: Your team also keeps one master workbook. Once a week, at the team meeting, you open the EXPORT sheet here and paste its numbers into your row on the master's TEAM sheet, then paste your log rows into the master's shared logs. That is the whole handover.

about.label: Fill in SETUP first
about.text: Your name and matric number on SETUP are what the EXPORT sheet stamps onto your numbers, so the team can tell whose row is whose.

about.label: Colour convention
about.text: AMBER cells are yours to fill in. GREY cells are calculated - typing over one breaks the summary that depends on it.

about.label: The honest bit
about.text: This file is the evidence behind your individual mark. Logging work you did not do is academic dishonesty, and because the master cross-checks your reported hours against the rows you paste in, a workbook that disagrees with itself is visible immediately.

routine: Every working session:  start a LOGT row when you sit down, close it when you get up.
Every defect you fix:   a LOGD row, with the phase the mistake was made in.
Every test you run:     a LOGTEST row.
Every AI-assisted change: a LOGAI row, with a teammate named as reviewer.
Every week at the meeting: open EXPORT, paste into the master, done.

consolidation.label: Consolidate Plans
consolidation.text: Do this at the weekly meeting, with all five workbooks open.   1.  Each member opens their own workbook and goes to its EXPORT sheet - the numbers there are already calculated.   2.  Copy the row of six values and Paste Special > Values into columns F to K of your row above.   3.  Paste your log rows into the shared logs here (LOGT, LOGD, LOGTEST, LOGAI) so the team summaries and charts include your work.   4.  Check the Agrees? column. Green means the two sides match; anything else means somebody's work is recorded in one place and not the other, and the team plan is wrong until it is fixed.

consolidation.label: Make copies of the workbook for the team
consolidation.text: Do this once, at the launch.   1.  Fill SETUP and FORM-SI in this master first - the filenames in column E above are built from the team name and each matric number.   2.  Take the blank member workbook (TSPi_Member_Workbook_TMA3084_v3.0.xlsx), save one copy per member under the filename shown in column E, and fill in the name and matric on its SETUP sheet.   3.  Commit all of them to the repository under docs/tspi/ so the team and the instructor can see them.   4.  From then on, each member logs only in their own file and consolidates weekly.

consolidation.label: Why there is no button here
consolidation.text: The 2002 workbook used Visual Basic macros for these two jobs. This one does not: a macro-enabled file is blocked by default in current Excel, refuses to run on a Mac without extra permission, and does nothing at all in Google Sheets or LibreOffice, which is where a lot of this class works. Two minutes of copy and paste at the weekly meeting is slower, but it works everywhere and it puts the team in front of its own numbers once a week, which is the point of the meeting.

sample.note: WORKED SAMPLE  -  all names, matric numbers, emails, phone numbers and the client are fictional. The time, task and defect data is migrated from a real past team's workbooks with identities removed; the test, AI, client, GitHub and evaluation forms are illustrative, written to show what a complete workbook looks like. Do not copy the numbers - copy the habit.

charter.label: Team vision
charter.text: Give SeaFresh's counter staff a phone app that replaces the paper order book, so an order reaches the kitchen without being re-typed.

charter.label: Communication norms
charter.text: WhatsApp group for day-to-day, GitHub Issues for anything that needs a record. Replies within 12 hours on weekdays. Stand-up every Wednesday 4pm in the lab; client meeting every second Saturday.

charter.label: Definition of done
charter.text: Merged to develop, reviewed and approved by someone other than the author, tests written and passing, CI green, and the LOGAI row filled in if a generator touched it.

charter.label: Conflict resolution
charter.text: Raise it in the Wednesday meeting first. If the team cannot settle it, the Team Leader decides and records the reason in IRTL. Nobody re-opens a settled decision without new information.

charter.label: Quality standards
charter.text: 60% coverage on business logic, zero analyzer warnings on develop, code review within 24 hours, and no AI-generated code merged without a second pair of eyes.

charter.label: Commitment
charter.text: About 10 hours per person per week. Tell the team in advance if you will be away; an unexplained silent week gets raised at the next meeting.
